doc.title: Ray Blue interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 23, 2022

chapter: The blues and the jazz economy
title: Ministry of Culture and jazz in the marketplace
summary: Blue contrasts European state arts support with the US and says artists must find ways to make it work.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: because we play the music. Okay? I think that’s just something to think about. We are, I don’t know if we’re the only country, modern country, who doesn’t have a Ministry of Culture. Okay? All these Western European countries have a Ministry of Culture where artists are supported. You know? It’s built into their culture. Ours is built-in differently. You know? There’s a whole — I don’t know — do you understand what I’m saying? They have a Ministry of Culture it’s part of the government system. So if an artist — that’s how important our culture is in that if you’re having hard times earning the money you can get government support because you’re an artist, to help sustain you to continue to do what you do, because you contribute something that’s valuable. You know? We have to go about it another way here in America. We have to find support from other places. You know? And we have to look for them. It’s not offered to us because we’re artists. We have to find it then make application for it, da-da-da-da-da. We have to find supporters and entrepreneurs and philanthropists to help us through. It’s not like that in a lot of other places. And I equate that to how they respect the necessity for art within the culture.

Jazz in particular in the last thirty or so years has been elevated, rightfully so, in academia and Jazz at Lincoln Center, on and on. It doesn’t seem to translate to a place in the marketplace. It’s a bit of a conundrum it seems like.

Um hum. Yeah. It is, however, we find a way to make it work. You know? There’s one thing that’s said about the human condition and that is people will get used to anything. All right? So our situation, okay it’s what it is. I’m used to it and here’s what I do to make it work for me, to continue to do what I do. That’s how I look at it. It’s the condition and I have to adapt to the condition. Otherwise I don’t exist. And I’m not having that. You know? So yeah, so we find way to make things work. I created a not- for-profit organization, a 501(c)3. And we don’t get a lot of — we don’t apply for a lot of grants. We’ve been in operation for sixteen years or so. We run our own festival etcetera. The people support it. The people support the music. We get donations, some grants, but it’s the people who support our organization and we are able to teach, we go out and we do workshops and clinics, master classes. We have an intergenerational ensemble. We have our own annual jazz festival, we have a weekly jazz series every Saturday throughout the summer and into the fall, and the people support it.
